examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
examples.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x =2\tan{t}, \, y =3\sec{t}.$
examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\tan{t}$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\sec{t}$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity $\tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0,\pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,4)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=4.$

Recall also that the asymptotes of the hyperbola occur at $y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{4}{5}x.
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{b} & =\frac{4}{5} \\ b & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=5\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$
